facts.fact_text: On 22 April 2000, the applicant organised a demonstration in Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul.
The demonstration organised by the applicant on 22 April 2000 took the form of a march followed by a statement to the press.
At about 12 noon on 22 April 2000, a group of forty to fifty persons gathered in Sultanahmet Square brandishing placards and signs.
The group of forty to fifty persons gathered in Sultanahmet Square under the leadership of the applicant and Eren Keskin.
The demonstrators refused to obey the police order to disperse.
The police asked the group gathered in Sultanahmet Square to disperse and to end the gathering.
The police dispersed the group of demonstrators using a kind of tear gas known as 'pepper spray'.
The police arrested thirty-nine demonstrators, including the applicant.
In her criminal complaint of 26 April 2000, the applicant alleged that she had been prevented from making the public statement scheduled for the end of the demonstration.
The police informed the group via a loudspeaker that the demonstration was likely to cause public-order problems at a busy time of day.
The police dispersed the group of demonstrators using a kind of tear gas known as 'pepper spray'.

It is recognised that the use of 'pepper spray' can produce effects such as respiratory problems, nausea, vomiting, irritation of the respiratory tract, irritation of the tear ducts and eyes, spasms, chest pain, dermatitis, or allergies.
It is recognised that in strong doses, 'pepper spray' may cause necrosis of tissue in the respiratory or digestive tract.
It is recognised that in strong doses, 'pepper spray' may cause pulmonary oedema.
It is recognised that in strong doses, 'pepper spray' may cause internal haemorrhaging, specifically haemorrhaging of the suprarenal gland.

The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission) adopted an opinion interpreting the OSCE/ODHIR guidelines on drafting laws on freedom of assembly with regard to the regulation of public meetings at its 64th plenary session held on 21-22 October 2005.
The Venice Commission's opinion set out its approach particularly with regard to advance notice of demonstrations in public places.

The Venice Commission stated in paragraph 29 of its opinion that establishing a regime of prior notification of peaceful assemblies does not necessarily extend to an infringement of the right to freedom of assembly, and that such regimes exist in several European countries.

The Venice Commission stated in paragraph 29 of its opinion that the need for advance notice generally arises in respect of certain meetings or assemblies — for instance, when a procession is planned to take place on the highway, or a static assembly is planned to take place on a public square — which require the police and other authorities to enable it to occur and not to use powers that they may validly have (for instance, of regulating traffic) to obstruct the event.

The Venice Commission emphasised in paragraph 30 of its opinion that the regime of prior notification must not in any circumstances indirectly restrict the right to hold peaceful meetings by, for instance, providing for too detailed and complicated requirements, or imposing too onerous procedural conditions.
